We have wheat to spare in our granary, and it is our way to deal fairly with strangers. If they truly hunger, we would share what the earth has given us. But I will not send my people wandering the deep forests on a shadow's word. Show me the path to their fires, and we shall see if your words hold truth.

I know the wind. It cools the brow during the harvest and bites the skin in the lean moons, but it does not have a mouth to speak. 

My people are joyful, and we have grain enough to feed our children until they grow into elders. Yet the mind is always hungry for new ways to keep what we have gathered. We have seen that the eiqua mud drinks the fire's heat and grows hard enough to hold water. If you truly move over all the world, tell me how we might shape this earth to our use. Otherwise, blow on and leave a chief to his rest.

You speak to me of neighbours we have never seen. The night air brings many whispers, and a chief cannot feed his people on shadows and dreams. 

We have much xi wheat stored from our harvests, more than enough to share. I am a fair man, and I know well that a starving stranger soon becomes a desperate raider, so I would gladly trade. But where does this Joawethom lie? Tell me the true path my scouts must walk, and if they find real men there, we will bring them grain.

I feel the wind in my waking hours, spirit, but it carries many shifting voices, and I do not know if you are one I should trust. If you are the breath that blows over our roofs, you see a joyful village with full grain bins, yet my mind must turn now to the earth, for spring is the time to plant our xi wheat. 

Our crafters have spent a season trying to find some new wisdom in the warm mantle and the drum, but they have learned nothing. Since you wander so freely, tell me: what new craft or ingredient should my people try instead, or what distant strangers have you seen across the waters?

You speak of Joawethom, a name my scouts have never brought back to our fires. It is true our granaries are heavy with xi wheat, and our village knows good times, but dreams are like river mist—shifting and unsure. 

I am a fair man, and I will not let strangers starve if we have food to share. But I must know if your words are true before I send my people walking with heavy baskets. If these people truly walk the earth, tell me which way the wind blows to reach them. Where does this Joawethom lie?
